questions.stem_markdown: A 15-year-old says, "I only vape, and at least I'm not smoking cigarettes." Which response is **most appropriate**?

options.text: If cigarettes are not being smoked, vaping can usually be left out of adolescent risk assessment.
Vaping still matters because e-cigarette use is rising in adolescents and is associated with later uptake of traditional cigarettes.
E-cigarettes only become relevant when they are used with cannabis.
The key question is only whether his parents smoke.
Because smoking rates are declining overall, vaping is not a meaningful adolescent concern.

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes state that e-cigarettes are on the rise in adolescents and that those who use e-cigarettes are three times more likely to take up traditional cigarettes. That makes vaping worth addressing even when the young person is not currently smoking cigarettes.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes treat e-cigarettes as part of adolescent substance-use review, not something to ignore until cigarette smoking appears.
why_others_wrong.C: The relevance of e-cigarettes in the notes does not depend on concurrent cannabis use.
why_others_wrong.D: Parental smoking can matter, but the notes specifically identify vaping itself as an important adolescent trend.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes say smoking and alcohol use are declining overall, but e-cigarettes are rising, so this conclusion is the opposite of the note-based message.

key_takeaways: E-cigarette use is increasing in adolescents.
Vaping still belongs in routine adolescent substance-use assessment.
Note-based counselling can mention the association between e-cigarette use and later traditional cigarette uptake.

questions.stem_markdown: A 16-year-old says, "I only drink at parties, so it's just social and not really a health issue." Which response is **best supported** by the notes?

options.text: Even social drinking matters in adolescence because risky consumption remains high, adolescents are more likely to binge drink, mix alcohol with other substances and experience harms, and early onset is linked to later problems.
Alcohol mainly becomes concerning once daily use begins.
Party drinking is usually low risk if school attendance remains good.
Early alcohol use has little bearing on later mental health, memory or concentration.
Social drinking is less relevant than vaping because alcohol use is declining.

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes emphasise that risky alcohol use remains common in adolescence and that adolescents are more likely to binge drink, mix alcohol with other substances, have withdrawal and suffer harms. They also state that early onset alcohol use increases later problematic use, adult alcohol dependence, mental health issues and memory and concentration problems.

why_others_wrong.B: The notes do not limit concern to daily use; they specifically discuss risky adolescent drinking patterns and harms.
why_others_wrong.C: Good school attendance does not rule out the alcohol-related risks described in the notes.
why_others_wrong.D: This directly contradicts the notes, which link early onset alcohol use with mental health issues and memory and concentration problems.
why_others_wrong.E: Declining overall use does not make alcohol unimportant; the notes still describe high levels of risky alcohol consumption in adolescents.

key_takeaways: Alcohol can still be clinically important even when described as social or party use.
Adolescents are vulnerable to binge drinking, polysubstance use and alcohol-related harms.
Early onset drinking is linked to later problematic use and cognitive and mental health impacts.

questions.stem_markdown: A 17-year-old says she uses cannabis before bed because it "treats" her anxiety. Which response is **most appropriate**?

options.text: If cannabis feels calming, it is unlikely to contribute to later mental health problems.
Cannabis used for sleep is less relevant than daytime use because it does not affect cognition.
Because she is using it for a symptom, formal substance-use screening is unnecessary.

Some adolescents use cannabis to self-medicate anxiety or depression, but early cannabis use is linked to cognitive harms and anxiety, depression and psychosis, so both the anxiety and the cannabis use should be explored.
Cannabis is mainly a concern only when there is obvious dependence.

questions.explanation_markdown: The CAH Bible notes that cannabis may be used to self-medicate anxiety and depression, but Louisa states that early-onset cannabis increases the risk of impaired attention, IQ, memory and concentration, as well as anxiety, depression and psychosis. The best response is therefore to explore both the presenting symptoms and the cannabis use rather than accepting the young person's explanation at face value.

why_others_wrong.A: This is too reassuring and ignores the mental health risks linked to early cannabis use in the notes.
why_others_wrong.B: The notes link cannabis with cognitive harms and do not suggest night-time use is benign.
why_others_wrong.C: Using cannabis for a symptom does not make screening unnecessary; it is one reason to assess more carefully.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes support earlier counselling and assessment rather than waiting for obvious dependence.

key_takeaways: Some adolescents use cannabis to self-medicate anxiety or depression.
Early cannabis use is linked to cognitive harms and adverse mental health outcomes.
Counselling should address both the symptom being managed and the substance use itself.

questions.stem_markdown: A 14-year-old who has tried alcohol twice asks why you keep asking about alcohol and vaping when he is "obviously not addicted." What is the **best explanation**?

options.text: Prevention conversations are mainly for young people who already have withdrawal or dependence.
Experimentation in early adolescence is too common to be clinically useful.
Asking early is appropriate because adolescence is a peak age of substance initiation and the developing brain is susceptible to the addictive effects of alcohol and other drugs.
Screening can wait until use patterns are fully established in late adolescence.
Alcohol and vaping only become relevant once they are clearly affecting memory or concentration.

questions.explanation_markdown: Louisa notes that adolescence is a peak age of initiation of substance use and that the developing brain is susceptible to the addictive effects of alcohol and other drugs. That supports early prevention-focused questioning rather than waiting for clear dependence or harm to emerge.

why_others_wrong.A: The notes support early screening and prevention, not waiting for withdrawal or dependence.
why_others_wrong.B: Common experimentation does not make it clinically irrelevant; it is one reason adolescent prevention matters.
why_others_wrong.D: This delays assessment in a way that is inconsistent with the note-based emphasis on early initiation and risk.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes support earlier prevention-focused review rather than waiting for obvious cognitive effects.

key_takeaways: Adolescence is a peak period for initiating substance use.
The adolescent brain is vulnerable to addictive effects.
Early questioning is part of prevention, not only a response to established dependence.

questions.stem_markdown: A 15-year-old says he "hardly ever drinks" but sometimes accepts rides home from older friends after parties. Which additional question from a validated adolescent substance-use screen most directly addresses this immediate safety issue?

options.text: Have you ever ridden in a car driven by someone under the influence of drugs or alcohol?
Have you ever used drugs or alcohol to relax or fit in?
Have you ever used drugs or alcohol while alone?
Have you ever forgotten anything while using drugs or alcohol?
Have your friends or family told you to cut down?

questions.explanation_markdown: This is the 'Car' item from CRAFFT and directly targets an immediate substance-related safety risk. In a young person who minimises their own use but describes risky transport situations around parties, it is a highly relevant next screening question.

why_others_wrong.B: This is also a CRAFFT item, but it does not address the immediate transport-related safety issue raised in the stem as directly as the car question.
why_others_wrong.C: Using substances while alone is concerning, but it is not the most direct screen for the immediate safety risk described.
why_others_wrong.D: Memory blackouts matter, but this does not most directly address the risky ride-home situation in the scenario.
why_others_wrong.E: Advice from others to cut down may signal concern, but it does not directly screen the transport danger highlighted in the stem.

key_takeaways: CRAFFT includes a question about riding in a car driven by someone under the influence.
Substance-use screening should include immediate safety risks, not just the young person's own consumption.
Minimisation of use does not remove the need for targeted screening.

questions.stem_markdown: A 17-year-old denies cannabis or other drug use but describes repeated heavy drinking on weekends. You want to add an alcohol-specific screen for dependence rather than a broad mixed-substance screen. Which tool **best matches** that aim?

options.text: CRAFFT
AUDIT-C
HEEADSSS
Brief interventions (5 A's)
Neurocognitive assessment

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes state that AUDIT or AUDIT-C may be used to screen for alcohol dependence specifically, whereas CRAFFT is the broader adolescent substance-use screen. That makes AUDIT-C the best match for an alcohol-focused screen in this scenario.

why_others_wrong.A: CRAFFT is useful for broad alcohol and drug screening, but the notes reserve AUDIT-C for alcohol dependence specifically.
why_others_wrong.C: HEEADSSS is a broad psychosocial assessment, not an alcohol dependence screening tool.
why_others_wrong.D: The 5 A's are a brief intervention framework, not a screening instrument.
why_others_wrong.E: Neurocognitive assessment is part of broader evaluation, not an alcohol-specific dependence screen.

key_takeaways: AUDIT-C is the note-supported alcohol-specific screening tool.
CRAFFT is broader and covers alcohol and other drugs.
Tool choice should match the clinical question being asked.

questions.stem_markdown: During review, a 16-year-old answers 'yes' to using alcohol to relax or fit in, using substances while alone, and forgetting things while using them. What is the **best interpretation**?

options.text: This pattern can be ignored if the young person is still passing at school.
These answers are only significant if there has also been police trouble.
These are concerning CRAFFT responses and support a fuller adolescent drug and alcohol assessment rather than reassurance alone.
The answers suggest cannabis withdrawal rather than broader substance risk.
CRAFFT is mainly a vaping screen, so alcohol-related answers are less useful.

questions.explanation_markdown: The stem describes several positive CRAFFT domains. In the notes, CRAFFT sits within a broader adolescent substance-use assessment, and positive findings should lead into a more comprehensive review of risks, harms and comorbidities rather than simple reassurance.

why_others_wrong.A: Stable school marks do not make these responses reassuring; the pattern still warrants fuller assessment.
why_others_wrong.B: Police trouble is only one possible domain of concern and is not required before the screen becomes meaningful.
why_others_wrong.D: The features described are screening responses about substance-related behaviours, not a withdrawal syndrome.
why_others_wrong.E: CRAFFT is a general adolescent alcohol and drug screen, not a vaping-only tool.

key_takeaways: Multiple positive CRAFFT responses should prompt further assessment.
Screening is the start of evaluation, not the endpoint.
Passing at school does not rule out significant substance-related risk.

questions.stem_markdown: You have asked about a 16-year-old's daily vaping and assessed her stage of change and possible dependence. According to the 5 A's framework in the notes, what is the **best next step**?

options.text: Arrange routine follow-up first, then discuss quitting later.
Skip straight to neurocognitive testing.
End the conversation unless she specifically requests treatment.
Advise her to quit.
Limit the discussion to what her friends are doing.

questions.explanation_markdown: The brief intervention sequence in the notes is Ask, Assess, Advise, Assist, Arrange. Once asking and assessment have been completed, the next step is to advise quitting rather than ending the discussion or jumping past the advice step.

why_others_wrong.A: Arrange comes after advising and assisting; it is not the next step once Ask and Assess are done.
why_others_wrong.B: Neurocognitive testing is not the next step in the 5 A's brief intervention sequence.
why_others_wrong.C: The framework supports active brief intervention, not stopping the conversation at this point.
why_others_wrong.E: Peers may be relevant context, but this does not replace the next brief-intervention step.

key_takeaways: The 5 A's proceed in sequence: Ask, Assess, Advise, Assist, Arrange.
Advice to quit is a core part of brief intervention.
Readiness assessment does not replace clear advice.

questions.stem_markdown: A 17-year-old wants help stopping vaping. You have already asked about use, assessed readiness and dependence, and clearly advised quitting. Which next plan **best fits** the brief intervention model in the notes?

options.text: Assist with cessation support and arrange follow-up.
Provide psychoeducation only and stop there.
Arrange review only, because assistance should wait until the young person has already stopped.
Switch the conversation to school performance only.
Repeat the same advice at a later visit without offering support.

questions.explanation_markdown: After Ask, Assess and Advise, the notes move to Assist and Arrange. They also give nicotine replacement therapy as an example of assistance. That makes supported cessation help plus follow-up the best next plan.

why_others_wrong.B: Psychoeducation may help, but the 5 A's framework specifically moves on to assisting and arranging follow-up after advice.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes do not say assistance should wait until abstinence has already been achieved.
why_others_wrong.D: School performance may be relevant, but it does not replace assistance and follow-up once the young person wants help.
why_others_wrong.E: Repeating advice later without offering support does not fit the Assist and Arrange steps in the model.

key_takeaways: Assist and Arrange follow Advise in the 5 A's model.
The notes give nicotine replacement therapy as an example of assistance.
Follow-up planning is part of brief intervention, not an optional extra.

questions.stem_markdown: A 15-year-old presents after escalating weekend alcohol use, daily vaping, and recent cannabis use. He has become withdrawn and his school performance is falling. What is the **most appropriate next approach**?

options.text: An AUDIT-C score alone, because mental health and safety can wait until alcohol is addressed.
Immediate neurocognitive testing before taking a broader history.
A brief warning about addiction and discharge if he promises to cut down.
Psychoeducation alone as the whole response, without broader assessment or follow-up.

A comprehensive adolescent drug and alcohol assessment with engagement and confidentiality, HEEADSSS, substance-use screening, assessment of harms and mental health comorbidity, and consideration of child protection in a trauma-informed framework.

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes outline a comprehensive adolescent drug and alcohol assessment that includes engagement and confidentiality, HEEADSSS, substance-use assessment with tools such as CRAFFT or AUDIT-C, risks and harms, mental health comorbidities, child protection issues, and a trauma-informed framework. That is the best next approach in a young person with multisubstance use and broader psychosocial change.

why_others_wrong.A: AUDIT-C alone is too narrow for a case involving vaping, cannabis, school change and broader psychosocial concerns.
why_others_wrong.B: Neurocognitive assessment may have a role, but it should not replace the broader first-line adolescent assessment described in the notes.
why_others_wrong.C: A warning and discharge would miss the fuller assessment of harms, comorbidity and safety needs.
why_others_wrong.D: Psychoeducation alone would be incomplete in a young person with multisubstance use and functional decline.

key_takeaways: Substance-use assessment in adolescents should be broader than a single score.
Confidential engagement, psychosocial review and mental health comorbidity assessment matter.
Child protection and trauma-informed care may need to be considered in complex presentations.

questions.stem_markdown: A 16-year-old stopped daily cannabis use 4 days ago. Since then he has been irritable, restless, eating poorly, and having vivid dreams. Which explanation **best fits** the notes?

options.text: Typical acute cannabis intoxication
Cannabis withdrawal
Delayed sleep phase disorder
Alcohol dependence
Normal adolescent mood variability

questions.explanation_markdown: Louisa lists common cannabis withdrawal symptoms as anger, aggression, irritability, anxiety or nervousness, anorexia, weight loss, sleeping difficulties including vivid dreams, restlessness and depressed mood. The cluster in the stem fits cannabis withdrawal closely.

why_others_wrong.A: Acute cannabis effects are described differently and do not fit this post-cessation withdrawal pattern.
why_others_wrong.C: Sleep phase disorder does not explain the broader cluster of irritability, poor appetite and vivid dreams after stopping cannabis.
why_others_wrong.D: The stem points to recent cessation of daily cannabis rather than a primary alcohol problem.
why_others_wrong.E: The symptom pattern is too specific and temporally linked to stopping cannabis to dismiss as normal variability.

key_takeaways: Cannabis withdrawal can present after stopping regular use.
Irritability, anorexia, restlessness and vivid dreams are note-supported withdrawal features.
Temporal linkage to cessation helps distinguish withdrawal from background adolescent distress.

questions.stem_markdown: A 17-year-old presents shortly after using cannabis. Which additional feature would support **acute cannabis effects** rather than cannabis withdrawal?

options.text: Vivid dreams
Depressed mood
Conjunctival injection
Weight loss
Anorexia

questions.explanation_markdown: The CAH Bible lists conjunctival injection as an acute effect of cannabis, whereas the Louisa notes list anorexia, weight loss, depressed mood and sleeping difficulties including vivid dreams among withdrawal symptoms. That makes conjunctival injection the best discriminator here.

why_others_wrong.A: Vivid dreams are listed in the notes as part of cannabis withdrawal.
why_others_wrong.B: Depressed mood is a withdrawal feature in the Louisa notes, not the best marker of acute effect here.
why_others_wrong.D: Weight loss aligns with withdrawal rather than acute cannabis effects.
why_others_wrong.E: Anorexia is also listed as a withdrawal symptom.

key_takeaways: Acute cannabis effects and cannabis withdrawal have different clinical patterns.
Conjunctival injection supports acute cannabis effects.
Anorexia, weight loss, depressed mood and vivid dreams fit withdrawal more closely.
